questions.prompt: A festival programme sets its information out in four columns: Play · Troupe · Venue · Dates. Which question does the Venue column answer?

options.text: In which place is the play performed?
By which company is the play performed?
On which evenings is the play performed?
For which age group is the play intended?

questions.explanation: A venue is the place where a public event is held, so this is the column a reader consults when he wants to know where to go. Beside it, the troupe column names the people who perform and the dates column gives the evenings on which they do it — three different questions, three different columns, and a reader who confuses them arrives at the wrong door on the wrong night. Nothing in these four columns says who a show is meant for; a programme that limits an audience by age prints that separately, as a warning.

questions.prompt: A pupil's note-book carries this line about a Welsh actress: "1968 — joined a touring troupe; six years in village halls". Which sentence develops the note without adding anything to it?

options.text: 1968: joined a touring troupe, then six years of village halls.
In 1968 she joins a touring troupe, and she spends six years in village halls.
In 1968 she joined a touring troupe, and she spent six years in village halls.
In 1968 she joined a touring troupe, because village halls were the only work to be had.

questions.explanation: Developing a note means giving it back the three things it threw away — a subject, a verb, and a tense — while leaving its content untouched. A life that is over takes the past, so joins and spends belong to a story still going on and not to this one. A line that keeps its colon and its semicolon has not been developed at all: it is the note again, with a few more words. And the reason why the halls were the only work available appears nowhere in the note; a writer who supplies it has stopped reporting and started imagining.

questions.prompt: The linker "but" warns a reader that the second fact goes against what the first one led him to expect. In which of these pairs of notes does it really have that work to do?

options.text: left school at fifteen · found work in a printing shop the same year
trained for four years as a lawyer · never argued a single case
born in Sfax in 1930 · grew up in the streets of the old town
finished the play in 1962 · saw it staged two years afterwards

questions.explanation: Four years of training point straight at a career, so a man who never pleaded contradicts what his own preparation announced: that is the gap the linker is built for. The three other pairs hold no contradiction whatever. Leaving school and finding work belong together, as do being born in a town and growing up there, and both call for a simple addition. Writing a play and seeing it performed later is a sequence, which asks for a linker of time. Using this one where nothing is contradicted claims a tension the notes never mention, and an invented tension costs exactly what an invented date costs.

questions.prompt: You meet this line in a festival review: "The company is staging the play in a disused railway shed." Your dictionary splits the word into a noun part and a verb part. Which part do you read here, and what tells you so?

options.text: the noun part, since a stage is the floor of a theatre
the noun part, since the sentence describes a building
the verb part, since the word has more than one sense
the verb part, since staging is what the company does

questions.explanation: Before the meaning comes the job: in this line the word carries an -ing ending and follows is, which makes it the action the company is performing, so the verb half of the entry is the only half worth reading. Its senses are not those of the noun half, and taking the raised floor of a theatre as the meaning here leaves the sentence saying nothing. The shed is where the action happens, not proof that a noun is at work. And having several senses is true of the noun half quite as much, so it points to neither half.

questions.prompt: Working from a box of notes, a pupil produced this opening: "She won the national prize in 1994. Then she was born in Gabès in 1961, and after that she joined the drama club at her school." Every fact in it is true. What has gone wrong?

options.text: the verbs are in the past instead of the present
the facts do not come in the order they happened
the facts are joined without a single linker
two of the three facts are given without a date

questions.explanation: A prize handed out thirty-three years before the birth of the person who won it cannot be read, and the two linkers make it worse rather than better: each of them promises that what follows came next, and each of them is contradicted by the year printed beside it. Sorting the years back into line is the whole repair. The tense is not the fault here — a finished life is exactly what the past is for, and moving it into the present would be a second mistake on top of the first. Two linkers are present, and two of the three facts carry their year.
